nodes.text: You just hit a ball. Now the part nobody practices: where you stand while it travels.
You hit short and they step in, wide on the left. Where do you go before they swing?

options.label: Back to the center mark
options.reply: That leaves their sharp cross-court wide open. From the side, their angles are not even.

options.label: Stay put, you covered that side already
options.reply: Then you are guessing. One of their two replies turns into a long run.

options.label: A step past center, toward the cross-court side
options.reply: Yes. You cover their sharpest angle and still reach the line. Same short run either way.

nodes.text: Your opponent can only hit between their two widest shots. Stand halfway between those, not halfway across the court.
Both of their widest shots are drawn here. See how you stand a step right of center.

scene.caption: You hit short and they step in wide on the left. Their sharp cross-court is the shot that stretches you. So you recover a step right of center — the same short run to either reply.

nodes.text: How do you find that spot in a real rally?

options.label: From the ball they are hitting, cover their sharp cross-court
options.reply: That's it. Their most dangerous angle tells you which way to lean.

options.label: Watch their feet and copy the direction
options.reply: Their feet move late. By the time you read them, you are already sprinting.

nodes.text: Move the instant you finish your shot. Arriving late and still moving is what makes a ball feel out of reach.
You're thinking about position now. In doubles at the net, could you read the return before it's hit?
Every shot has two parts: the hit, and the walk to the middle of their angles.
Neutral rally. Nothing special is happening. Most people pick a direction here by accident.
You're balanced, the ball is comfortable, they're in the middle. Which ball do you hit?

options.label: Down the line, to move them
options.reply: You just aimed at the shortest court and the highest part of the net. Then you sprint diagonally to recover.

options.label: Short and low, to bring them in
options.reply: On a neutral ball that's an invitation. They step in and you spend the rest of the point defending.

options.label: Cross-court, deep
options.reply: Yes. Longest court, lowest net, and you finish the shot near your recovery spot.

nodes.text: The diagonal is about a meter and a half longer than the sideline. That is free margin on every swing.
The net is lower in the middle than at the posts. Cross-court crosses the low part.
Same swing, two targets. Look at how much more court the cross-court has to land in.

scene.caption: Same swing, two targets. The cross-court has more court to land in and a lower net to clear.

nodes.text: Down the line isn't banned. It's a shot you choose on purpose, not a place your racket ends up.
Default is cross-court and deep. Change it when you have a reason.
A floating ball comes to you at the baseline. You have time and you're balanced. This is where matches leak.
Swing hard at it, or three-quarter pace a meter inside their baseline?

options.label: Swing hard, pace is what hurts them
options.reply: A set opponent just borrows the pace you add. And the harder you swing, the smaller your margin gets.

options.label: Three-quarter pace, deep
options.reply: Right. Depth is what takes their options away, not speed.

options.label: Drop shot, they're standing back
options.reply: They're back but balanced, with time to read it. You'd be handing them a short ball to run onto.

nodes.text: From behind their own baseline they can barely make an angle. There is almost nothing there to hit.
The green band is deep with margin. The red band is where you invite an attack.

scene.caption: The green band is deep with margin. The red band lets them step in and attack.

nodes.text: So what do you aim at — the baseline itself?

options.label: Yes, the line, for maximum depth
options.reply: At the line you have no margin left. Half your normal spread of shots lands out.

options.label: About a meter inside it
options.reply: That's the band. Deep enough to push them back, safe enough to hit all afternoon.

nodes.text: Most beginner points aren't lost to a spectacular winner. They're lost to one short ball that invited one.
Deep beats hard. Aim past the service line, never at the baseline.
Deuce. You get a comfortable forehand in the middle of the court. They're in position and ready.
What's your target?

options.label: The corner, right where the lines meet
options.reply: Aim at a line and half your normal spread lands out. On a big point, that's a coin flip you didn't need.

options.label: A meter inside the sideline and inside the baseline
options.reply: Yes. They can't tell the difference. The scoreboard can.

options.label: At their feet, so they can't swing
options.reply: That's a short ball with a good excuse attached. They step in and take the court from you.

nodes.text: Lines are for spectators. Margin is for players.
The target sits inside the sideline and inside the baseline. Still wide enough to hurt them.

scene.caption: The target sits inside the sideline and inside the baseline — wide enough to hurt, safe enough to repeat.

nodes.text: Margin is vertical as well. A rally ball passing a meter above the net still lands deep, and never finds the tape.
So when do you actually paint a line?

options.label: When they're out of position and the point is nearly over
options.reply: That's the one. Lines are for finishing, not for building.

options.label: On big points, when you need something special
options.reply: Big points are exactly when you want the shot you can repeat. Special is how people donate them.

nodes.text: One meter inside every line, on every ball you aren't finishing.
You came forward, they lofted one back deep, and you're standing right on the service line.
What do you do?

options.label: Hold your ground and half-volley it
options.reply: You're too far back to volley and too far forward to let the ball come to you. Worst of both.

options.label: Move back behind the baseline and play it normally
options.reply: Yes. An awkward half-volley turns into an ordinary groundstroke.

options.label: One small step forward, hope for a short reply
options.reply: Hope isn't a court position. The ball is landing deep, and it lands at your feet.

nodes.text: Live behind your baseline, or inside the service line. The strip between them is where balls land at your feet.
Two good places to stand, and the strip in between that has no answer to anything.

scene.caption: Two good places to stand, and the strip between them where the ball always lands at your feet.

nodes.text: I raid bins for a living, and even I commit to a direction before I arrive.
So you stay out of that strip completely?

options.label: Yes, never set foot in it
options.reply: Then approach shots and drop shots are off the menu, and you never move forward all match.

options.label: Run through it, just never stop there
options.reply: Exactly. That strip is movement, not a position.

nodes.text: Behind the baseline or inside the service line. Never parked in between.
You've been dragged wide off the court. Your weight is going sideways and you're barely reaching the ball.
They're waiting in the middle of their baseline. What do you hit?

options.label: A sharp cross-court angle to get them moving
options.reply: Off balance you can't hit that reliably. Miss it and you've lost the point outright.

options.label: A high, deep ball down the middle
options.reply: Yes. It buys you the seconds you need and gives them nothing to work with.

options.label: A drop shot, you can't do much else
options.reply: Stretched and off court, that drop shot sits up short. They run onto it and you're still out of position.

nodes.text: Down the middle you clear the lowest part of the net. And you keep room on both sidelines.
You also keep a half-court of room on each side. There is no safer combination.
Pulled off court and out of position. The deep middle is the road back to neutral.

scene.caption: Pulled off court and out of position — the deep middle gets you back to neutral.

nodes.text: Why does the middle protect you as well?

options.label: It takes their angles away, no diagonal from there
options.reply: Right. Whatever comes back arrives in front of you, so you get your position back.

options.label: It surprises them, nobody covers the middle
options.reply: You're not tricking anyone from off balance. Surprise isn't what you need here.

nodes.text: Reset, don't rescue. Off balance is not the moment to go for a winner.
In trouble: high, deep, middle. Neutral is where you start building again.
Every ball that comes at you is one of three things. Most people work out which one halfway through the swing.
Their ball lands short and high with no pace. You're moving forward and you'll meet it above the net.

options.label: Neutral — deep cross-court, then wait
options.reply: Safe, and you just spent the best ball of the point on nothing. It won't come round again.

options.label: Attack — pick a target and follow it forward
options.reply: Yes. Short, high, slow, and you're already moving in. That's every attacking marker at once.

options.label: Defend — high and deep down the middle
options.reply: You're defending against nothing. That hands them a free reset from a ball they mishit.

nodes.text: Label the ball before you swing: attacking, neutral, defending. The label picks the shot for you.
Almost nobody loses a point to a bad shot. They lose it to a good shot on the wrong ball.
Roughly, where their ball lands decides which of the three shots you owe.

scene.caption: Roughly, where their ball lands decides which of the three shots you owe.

nodes.text: How do you get quicker at reading it?

options.label: Call the label out loud as it leaves their racket
options.reply: That's the drill. A few sessions and the read starts happening without you.

options.label: Decide once you've seen the bounce
options.reply: By the bounce you're already swinging. The decision arrives after the shot does.

nodes.text: Label first, swing second. That read is most of what people mean by tennis IQ.
A heavy ball comes cross-court to your backhand. You get there, just, weight still moving sideways.
Where do you hit it?

options.label: Down the line, to change the rally's direction
options.reply: You're reversing all that sideways speed with a stretched arm. It goes wide, or short into the middle.

options.label: Short and low, to kill their pace
options.reply: Off balance, that one sits up nearer the net than you meant. They're already running onto it.

options.label: Back cross-court, the way it came
options.reply: Yes. The ball keeps its own direction and your racket barely has to argue with it.

nodes.text: Redirecting a fast ball means reversing its sideways momentum with your racket face. That timing window is tiny.
Their diagonal, and your two replies. Only one of them asks nothing of your timing.

scene.caption: A hard cross-court arrives. Returning it along the same diagonal is the low-risk reply.

nodes.text: Sending it straight back feels unambitious. It's also the reason you're still in the point.
So when do you change direction?

options.label: On a slower ball, with time and both feet under you
options.reply: Right. Then the change of direction hurts them instead of hurting you.

options.label: When they least expect it
options.reply: Surprise doesn't buy you timing. The speed of the ball decides this one, not their guess.

nodes.text: Hard or late: send it back the same way. Change direction on a ball that lets you.
You've netted four rally balls in two games. Your swing feels fine and you're getting there in time.
What's the first thing you change?

options.label: Swing harder so the ball gets there faster
options.reply: A flat ball hit harder is still a flat ball. You'll just find the tape sooner.

options.label: Pass a meter or more above the net
options.reply: Yes. Net misses are a flight-path problem, and this fix costs you nothing.

options.label: Aim nearer the sidelines to shorten the rallies
options.reply: Now you can miss wide as well as into the net. Two ways to lose instead of one.

nodes.text: Count the misses in any club match. More of them go into the net than past the baseline.
Height buys depth as well. Same swing, higher path, and the ball lands further back.
Two versions of the same stroke. Watch which one runs out of court before the net.

scene.caption: The same stroke with more net clearance travels deeper and never finds the tape.

nodes.text: I clear every fence with a meter to spare. Not elegance. Margin.
Why does an arcing ball also bother them?

options.label: It drops from above shoulder height, with no easy contact point
options.reply: Right. Plenty of club players have no attacking answer to a ball falling on them.

options.label: It's slower, so they get impatient and rush
options.reply: You can't build a tactic on someone's mood. Whatever troubles them has to be physical.

nodes.text: A meter of air over the net on every rally ball. Flat is for finishing.
You're 3-5 down. The last two games went on a couple of winners and a lot more errors.
What change is most likely to win you the next game?

options.label: Go bigger, since the small shots aren't working
options.reply: Your errors are what's losing the games. Raising the stakes just produces them faster.

options.label: Hit one more deep ball than feels natural before attacking
options.reply: Yes. You keep the pressure on and let their mistakes decide the game.

options.label: Slow every ball down and just push it back
options.reply: Now you've stopped competing. They step in, take the court, and end it whenever they like.

nodes.text: At club level most points end in a mistake, not a winner. So the cheapest points come from making fewer.
Three honest balls, deep and unremarkable. Nothing in here is heroic.

scene.caption: Three honest balls. A lot of opponents run out of patience before you run out of shots.

nodes.text: Give yourself a number in practice. A few deep balls in a row before anyone is allowed to go for it.
Isn't that just pushing?

options.label: Yes, but it only works on weaker opponents
options.reply: Then you'd drop it against anyone good, which is exactly when errors decide the match.

options.label: No — the extra ball is still deep and high
options.reply: Right. You're refusing to donate the point while you wait for one you can attack.

nodes.text: Patience is the only athletic quality I have. It has never once let me down.
Be the player who hits one more. Most opponents run out of patience first.
Their ball is dying in the air. It is going to land around your service line.
You read it early and you can get there. What's the play?

options.label: Wait behind the baseline and let it come to you
options.reply: Then you're hitting up from below the net, on the run. A free ball turned into a hard one.

options.label: Move in, take it early, keep coming forward
options.reply: Yes. You stay above the ball, and you're already there for the next one.

options.label: Move in, hit it, then recover to the baseline
options.reply: You earned that court and handed it straight back. Now the whole point starts again.

nodes.text: A short ball isn't something to survive. It's the signal you've been waiting for all point.
Step in, hit it going forward, keep going. Look at where the shot starts.

scene.caption: Move to the short ball, hit it going forward, and keep coming.

nodes.text: The read starts at their strings, not at the bounce. Little pace and a low, dying arc means short.
You've stepped in and hit the approach. Where do you stand now?

options.label: Inside the service line, split step, ready to volley
options.reply: Yes. Finish forward. That's the whole reason you came in.

options.label: Back on the baseline, in case they get it back
options.reply: Walking backwards after an approach parks you where balls land at your feet.

nodes.text: Short ball means forward. Take it early and follow it in.
You've hit four straight balls to their backhand. Each reply came back shorter and weaker than the last.
The rally is still going. What do you do with the next ball?

options.label: Switch to the forehand so they can't settle
options.reply: You'd release four balls of pressure and hand them a comfortable one. That's a rest, not a tactic.

options.label: The backhand again
options.reply: Yes. It's getting worse every time you go there. Don't rescue them.

options.label: Go for a winner down the line and end it
options.reply: Nothing in this rally has offered you a ball worth finishing yet. You'd be finishing it for them.

nodes.text: For most developing players the backhand is the newer side. So it's your default target until they prove otherwise.
Against a right-hander, that's the corner you keep visiting.

scene.caption: Against a right-hander, that corner is the backhand — the default target until they prove it is not a weakness.

nodes.text: Hit a few to each wing in the first games. Then stop being fair.
What actually tells you a wing is the weaker one?

options.label: Short or floating replies, arriving again and again
options.reply: That's evidence. One ball proves nothing; six in a row produces something you can attack.

options.label: They look uncomfortable getting into position
options.reply: Plenty of players look awkward and still hit it clean. Their posture isn't evidence.

nodes.text: Beginners drop a working pattern out of boredom, usually one ball before it pays.
Backhand by default. When a pattern is working, get boring.
The serve is the one ball nobody can touch before you hit it. So of course everyone tries to crush it.
Count them for a week. Flat out, one first serve in three lands. Three-quarter pace, four in five. Which do you serve?

options.label: Flat out, a big serve wins free points
options.reply: Then two points out of three start with a second serve. That is where service games leak.

options.label: Switch, so they cannot read you
options.reply: Half your serves are still missing. Unreadable does not help when the ball lands long.

options.label: Three-quarter pace, to a target you picked
options.reply: Yes. Two first serves in a row is worth more than the speed you gave up for it.

nodes.text: Effort costs you accuracy before it buys you speed. Back off a notch and your timing window gets much wider.
Then name a target before you toss. T, body, or wide. Pick one.
Three targets in one service box. Choose before the toss, not during it.

scene.caption: Three targets in the deuce-court service box. Choose one before you toss.

nodes.text: And a serve you hit with no target in mind. Where does that one usually go?

options.label: Into the middle of the box
options.reply: Usually, yes. The one part of the box that pressures nobody.

options.label: Anywhere, which at least keeps them guessing
options.reply: You are guessing too. There is no plus-one shot after a serve you did not aim.

nodes.text: Three-quarter effort, one named target. A serve you can repeat beats a serve you can barely land.
Second serve. The first one missed, and now the safest-feeling thing in the world is to pat one in.
It is 30-30. They have stepped in on your slow middle serve all match. What do you hit?

options.label: Slower and safer, just guarantee it lands
options.reply: That is the ball they have been eating all match, only easier. They step in and the point is theirs.

options.label: Spin with net clearance, deep to the backhand
options.reply: Yes. Safe because of the spin, not because it is slow.

options.label: A second flat serve. If it lands, they cannot touch it
options.reply: If. At 30-30 that is a double fault waiting, and you hand the point over without a rally.

nodes.text: Safety on a second serve comes from spin and height over the net. Not from taking the pace off.
A soft ball landing near the service line is the easiest thing in tennis to attack.
Aim at the back third of the box. The front of the box is an invitation.

scene.caption: A serve into the back of the box keeps the returner honest. The front of the box invites an attack.

nodes.text: Deep to the backhand, or wide and a bit short?

options.label: Wide, the angle drags them off court
options.reply: A wide second serve that lands short gives them a short ball and an angle to hit back. You would be helping.

options.label: Deep, even if it is less wide
options.reply: Right. Depth is what keeps them behind their baseline and off your first rally ball.

nodes.text: I raid the same bin every night. Boring, repeatable, no surprises. Your second serve should feel like that.
In, deep, to the backhand. Never nudge one gently into the middle of the box.
Most people serve and then wait to see what comes back. That is not a play, that is a hope.
You serve wide in the deuce court. They are stretched outside their sideline. Where is your next ball going?

options.label: Straight back at them, before they recover
options.reply: You are hitting to the one spot they are already standing in. The empty half of the court stays empty.

options.label: Into the open court on the other side
options.reply: Yes. That space is the whole reason you served wide.

options.label: Short, to bring them forward
options.reply: A short ball invites them into the court you were about to hit into. You gave the space back.

nodes.text: A stretched returner usually sends it back through the middle, or crosscourt. Either way it is predictable, and you can already be moving.
Serve, their reply, your plus-one. Three balls you decided on before the toss.

scene.caption: A wide serve pulls them off court. Their reply comes back middle or crosscourt. Your plus-one goes into the space they left.

nodes.text: How many of these patterns do you need?

options.label: Two. Wide then open court, T then open side
options.reply: Two practiced patterns will carry a whole match. Two you trust, not six you half know.

options.label: One for every serve you own
options.reply: Then you are choosing between six plans while the ball is in the air. You will pick none of them.

nodes.text: Decide before you toss. Deciding after the return arrives is just reacting, with extra steps.
The serve is not the play. The serve plus the next ball is the play.
The return is the shot people most want to be a winner. It almost never is.
Their first serve is fast but lands mid-box. You reach it fine, with no time to swing. What do you hit?

options.label: A full swing cross-court, to take charge
options.reply: Off a fast serve a full swing is mostly a miss. A missed return is a point you gave away for free.

options.label: A soft high ball, to buy yourself time
options.reply: That floats. They step in and hit it before you have finished recovering.

options.label: A short compact block, deep down the middle
options.reply: Yes. You are borrowing their pace, not making your own.

nodes.text: A return that lands deep takes away the server's plus-one shot. That alone makes it a good return.
Through the middle they have no cross-court angle to use. The rally starts even, instead of with you defending.
Deep and central. Not clever, just the return that keeps you in the point.

scene.caption: Deep and central. This return neutralizes a serve instead of gambling on it.

nodes.text: So winners off the return, never?

options.label: A bonus when the serve is weak, never the plan
options.reply: That is it. Take the free one when it shows up. Do not go hunting for it.

options.label: Go for them, the return is your best chance to attack
options.reply: You would be gambling on the ball you have least time for. Missed returns are the cheapest points you can hand over.

nodes.text: In play, deep, near the middle. That return has already done its whole job.
Watch a club match and the returner stands in one spot all afternoon. First serve, second serve, same place.
They just missed a first serve. Their second is slow and lands short. Where do you stand for it?

options.label: Where you always stand, moving risks mistiming it
options.reply: Then a slow short ball gets to bounce and drop, and you play it from behind your own baseline anyway.

options.label: Two steps back, to be safe on a slow ball
options.reply: Safe from a serve that was never dangerous. You gave up the one ball you could have taken early.

options.label: Step in, about a step inside the baseline
options.reply: Yes. Step in about a step and take it early. They get to watch you do it.

nodes.text: Back for the first serve. That step or two is reaction time, and time is what you are short of.
In for the second. Earlier contact, less angle for them, and it all happens in front of their eyes.
Two positions, one per serve. The walk between them is the free part.

scene.caption: Two return positions. Moving between them is one of the cheapest ways to apply pressure.

nodes.text: What does the server see when you step in?

options.label: Nothing, they are busy with their own toss
options.reply: They are standing still, holding a ball, looking straight at your half of the court. They see it.

options.label: A returner who has decided something already
options.reply: That is the pressure. It costs you nothing and it arrives before the ball does.

nodes.text: I have never served in my life. I have watched a great many people stand perfectly still, though.
Back on firsts, in on seconds. Where you stand is a decision, not a habit.
Big point. This is the moment people reach for the serve they have been missing all afternoon.
It is 30-40 on your serve. Your body serve has landed all match, your wide one has mostly missed. Which?

options.label: The wide serve, aggressive and unexpected
options.reply: It has been missing all match. Unexpected does not help when the ball lands long.

options.label: The body serve to the backhand
options.reply: Yes. The one you actually have evidence for.

options.label: A very safe slow serve into the middle
options.reply: It lands, and then they attack it. You swapped a double fault for an easy ball against you.

nodes.text: A break point is decided by whether the ball goes in. Nothing else about it is special.
So know your best serve before you need it. Count them in practice. The target that lands most is yours.
One target you have proved, one you have not. On a break point, only one of them exists.

scene.caption: On a big point, aim where you have already proved you can land it.

nodes.text: So when do you try the untested one?

options.label: Early in a game, when a miss costs little
options.reply: Right. That is also what keeps your trusted serve unreadable later on.

options.label: Never, just stick with what works
options.reply: Then they read you by the third game and stand there waiting. The same serve every time is a pattern, not a weapon.

nodes.text: Serve your trusted target and accept a rally. A rally is a much better outcome than a double fault.
Big point, trusted target. Save the new one for when a miss is cheap.
The first two games aren't for winning. They're for collecting. Both wings, high and low, deep and short.
Second game. Their backhand looks messy, but every ball comes back deep.
Their textbook forehand floats short when you hit it high. Which side do you attack?

options.label: The backhand, the technique is clearly worse
options.reply: You'd be attacking the side that keeps returning deep balls. The swing looked bad; the result didn't.

options.label: High to the forehand, then attack the floater
options.reply: Yes. The short reply is the weakness, wherever it comes from.

options.label: Down the middle, wait for errors
options.reply: That's a hope, not a plan. You already found something and you're choosing to ignore it.

nodes.text: Judge the reply, not the stroke. Ugly and deep is fine. Pretty and short is a target.
I raid bins. Nothing in there is pretty, and some of it is excellent.
Four deliberate probes in the first two games. Watch what comes back off each one.

scene.caption: Four deliberate probes in the first two games. What comes back tells you the plan for the rest.

nodes.text: You've found the weak side. How often do you go there?

options.label: Until they solve it
options.reply: Right. Go there until they fix it. Nothing says you have to be fair.

options.label: Mix it around so they don't get grooved
options.reply: Go there until they solve it. One ball the other way now and then, only to stop them camping on it.

nodes.text: Two games of testing buys you an hour of knowing.
Between your shots there's a free second. Most players spend it watching their own ball travel.
You've dragged them wide to the backhand corner. They're sprinting back to the middle. Where do you hit?

options.label: The open court on the far side
options.reply: They are already sprinting that way. You would be hitting the ball right to them.

options.label: Back behind them, into the same corner
options.reply: Yes. Stop, turn, start again. That costs far more than a few extra steps.

options.label: Down the middle, keep the rally going
options.reply: You had them off balance and handed it straight back. Nothing you noticed got used.

nodes.text: Changing direction costs more than distance. A sprinting player has already committed their weight.
They're still moving back to the middle. The ball behind them makes them start over.

scene.caption: They are still moving back to the middle. The ball behind them makes them stop, turn and start again.

nodes.text: Against a slow recoverer, the same target twice is often enough. They're leaning away, waiting for the change.
I'm not an athlete. Even I can spot someone admiring their own shot.
So when do you make this read?

options.label: In the moment after the ball leaves their racket
options.reply: That's the window. Any later and you're picking a target by feel.

options.label: While they're still swinging, for more time
options.reply: Their feet haven't told you anything yet. You'd be guessing early instead of knowing late.

nodes.text: Look at their feet, then hit where they are not going.
They stand well behind the baseline and hit heavy. You've been trading with them and losing.
What actually changes this match?

options.label: Hit harder and deeper, push them further back
options.reply: That's the game they're built for. You'd be playing their rally, only worse.

options.label: Short and low, drag them forward, follow it in
options.reply: Yes. Forward is the direction nobody practices.

options.label: Slow it all down and rally patiently
options.reply: Against a heavy hitter, patience alone is a long wait for your own error.

nodes.text: Club players drill side to side for years. Almost nobody practices sprinting in to a low ball.
Nobody warms up by running forwards. Not them, not you, certainly not me.
Low matters as much as short. A short high ball is a gift; a low one makes them bend and lift.
Short and low, and you move in behind it. The weak reply lands near the net.

scene.caption: Low and short pulls a baseline player into the direction they never practice.

nodes.text: You've hit the short ball. Where are you standing?

options.label: Moving in behind it
options.reply: Right. The reply will be short and weak, and you need to be there for it.

options.label: Back at the baseline, ready for anything
options.reply: You brought them in and then gave the court back. The point resets, in their favour.

nodes.text: Forward is the hardest direction. Send them there, then follow.
Four balls long this game, and your swing felt completely normal. The wind is at your back.
What do you adjust?

options.label: Swing harder so the ball drops faster
options.reply: Harder sends it further, not sooner. The wind is helping the ball, not you.

options.label: Add topspin, keep it lower, aim shorter
options.reply: Yes. Topspin brings it down, and a shorter target soaks up the carry.

options.label: Same target, accept the errors
options.reply: Four in one game is not bad luck. That is the wind telling you something, twice.

nodes.text: Into the wind, do the opposite. Hit bigger and deeper, because the air holds the ball in.
I check which way the wind is going before I open a bin. Same idea.
The same swing, two wind directions, two different landing spots.

scene.caption: The same swing lands in two different places depending on which way the wind is going.

nodes.text: Sun is a read too. Note the end where it sits in the server's eyes.
Surface as well. Clay sits up and pays for patience. A fast court pays for the first strike.
When do you work all this out?

options.label: In the warm-up, before the first point
options.reply: That's it. Two minutes of noticing saves you a set of guessing.

options.label: After a few games, once you see a pattern
options.reply: By then the pattern is on the scoreboard. You paid for information that was free earlier.

nodes.text: Read the wind, the sun and the surface before the first point.
Break point, returning. All match, your deep cross-court to their backhand has worked.
You've also been thinking about that drop shot. You haven't landed one today.
What do you play?

options.label: The drop shot, surprise wins big points
options.reply: A shot you haven't landed all day is an experiment. Deuce is an expensive place to run one.

options.label: The deep cross-court to the backhand
options.reply: Yes. Boring and repeatable is exactly what a big point is for.

options.label: Whatever feels right when the ball arrives
options.reply: Feel is what you use when you have no plan. You have a plan.

nodes.text: Not all points weigh the same. 30-30, deuce, and break point decide games far more than 40-0 does.
I have one move. Tip the bin, run. Deeply dull, never once failed.
One pattern you trust, run on the point that actually decides the game.

scene.caption: On the points that decide games, run the pattern you already know works.

nodes.text: So where does the drop shot belong?

options.label: On the cheap points, like 40-0 or 40-15
options.reply: Exactly. Learn it there, when a lost point costs little, so it is ready when it is tight.

options.label: Saved for when nothing else is working
options.reply: Then it is a rescue shot you have never rehearsed. That is not a plan, it is panic.

nodes.text: Big point, boring pattern. Keep the interesting ideas for cheap points.
Down 1-4. You've traded deep baseline balls all set and lost most of the rallies.
What now?

options.label: Focus harder, commit to the same game
options.reply: Trying harder is not a change. You would lose the same rally with more effort in it.

options.label: One concrete change, run for a full game
options.reply: Yes. Something you can name, and then check.

options.label: Just swing harder and hope the misses stop
options.reply: That is effort, not a plan. You cannot name it or check it, so you learn nothing.

nodes.text: A change has to be nameable. A target, a height, a return position, where you stand to serve.
Then give it a full game. One point can't tell you whether it worked.
One thing you stop doing, one thing you start. Judge it a game later.

scene.caption: A change you can name and check: a different target, not just more effort.

nodes.text: Judge it by the balls coming back, not the score. Weaker replies mean it's working.
I once swapped a perfectly good bin for a new one. The new one was empty.
Next set you're up 4-1 with the same pattern. What do you change?

options.label: Nothing at all
options.reply: Right. Run it until they solve it. Boredom is not a tactical reason.

options.label: Add variety so they can't read you
options.reply: That's guilt, not tactics. You'd be fixing a problem they haven't managed to cause.

nodes.text: Losing, change one named thing. Winning, change nothing.
Time for patterns. Two balls, one plan, and the second ball is where the point is actually won.
You dragged them wide to their forehand corner. They are sprinting back to the middle. Where does your next ball go?

options.label: Cross-court into the open backhand side
options.reply: That is the space they are running into. The ball arrives in front of them at an easy height.

options.label: A drop shot to catch them out
options.reply: They are already sprinting forward toward the middle. Forward is the one way a drop shot does not hurt them.

options.label: Straight back into the same corner
options.reply: Yes. They have to stop, reverse, and start again. That is the expensive part.

nodes.text: The open court is only open until they get there. Hitting behind them turns their own momentum into the problem.
Changing direction at a sprint is costly. I have tried it on a fence, and the fence won.
Two balls to the same corner. Watch the second one arrive while they are still running away.

scene.caption: Two balls to the same corner. The second one arrives while they are running the other way.

nodes.text: When does this pattern stop working?

options.label: Once they have stopped and are balanced in the middle
options.reply: Right. Then they are waiting for it, and the open court is the better ball.

options.label: Once they expect it, so vary it every time
options.reply: Expecting it does not help them much. Vary it too early and you hand back a free point.

nodes.text: Depth does the work here, not pace. A deep ball stops them getting round it and swinging freely.
Wide, then behind. The second ball goes where they just were.
A slow ball drifts down the middle. This is the one ball where you get to choose your own weapon.
You are a right-hander, so are they. Your forehand is much better than your backhand. What do you do?

options.label: Take the backhand, the ball is on that side
options.reply: The ball is in the middle. Playing it with your weaker wing there is a choice, not an obligation.

options.label: Step around it and hit a forehand down the line
options.reply: Forehand, good. But down the line is the tighter target and the longer run home.

options.label: Step around it, forehand to their backhand
options.reply: Yes. Your best shot into their worst, on the safer diagonal.

nodes.text: Stand to the backhand side of the ball and swing across it. That sends a forehand into their backhand.
Watch the footwork first. The shot is ordinary; the step around the ball is the skill.

scene.caption: Move around the middle ball so your forehand — not your backhand — plays it.

nodes.text: I approach a bin from the side my paws can actually reach into. Same instinct, fewer trophies.
What does stepping around the ball cost you?

options.label: Your forehand corner is now wide open
options.reply: Exactly. Recover wider than feels natural, or their reply ends it.

options.label: Nothing, you are hitting from the middle anyway
options.reply: You started in the middle and finished several steps away. Something got left behind.

nodes.text: Middle ball, forehand, into their backhand. Then recover further than you want to.
This pattern makes them run two directions at once. Forward and sideways, in the same sprint.
It starts with a short angled cross-court off a comfortable ball. That drags them in and across.
It works. They are stranded near their service line on one side, scrambling the ball back. How do you finish?

options.label: Another short angle, same side
options.reply: That brings them back into the point. They are already standing next to it.

options.label: Deep down the open line, behind them
options.reply: Yes. The whole diagonal behind them is empty, and the ball only has to land in.

options.label: Hard straight at them so they cannot swing
options.reply: You would be feeding a volley to somebody already standing near the net.

nodes.text: Shot one pulls them in. Shot two goes to the space they left behind.

scene.caption: The short angle drags them forward and across. The deep line finishes into the space behind them.

nodes.text: When should you not try the short angle?

options.label: When you are defending or off balance
options.reply: Right. From there it lands short and central, and they take the attack off you.

options.label: When they are a quick mover
options.reply: Quick still has to cover forward and sideways at once. Speed is not what breaks this pattern.

nodes.text: The finish is not hit hard. Deep and inside the lines is unreachable from the service line.
Two directions at once is what breaks people. I can barely manage one.
Short cross to bring them in. Deep line to end it.
Coming forward is a pattern, not a mood. It has three parts, and everyone skips the middle one.
You hit a deep approach and you are running in. They start their swing. What do you do right now?

options.label: Keep sprinting, get as close to the net as possible
options.reply: A player still moving when the ball is struck cannot change direction. The ball finds your feet.

options.label: Split step and land balanced before contact
options.reply: Yes. Momentum becomes balance, and now you can go either way.

options.label: Stop and back up behind the baseline
options.reply: Then the approach shot was wasted, and you are defending from a worse spot than before.

nodes.text: A small hop as they swing, landing on both feet. That is the entire skill.
Deep ball, split step, volley. The stop in the middle is the part nobody practices.

scene.caption: Deep approach, split step inside the service line, then volley into the space.

nodes.text: Which of their balls invites you in?

options.label: A short one, near your service line
options.reply: Right. A short ball is the invitation. Your approach off it still has to land deep.

options.label: A deep one
options.reply: A deep ball keeps you honest at the baseline. It is not the one you attack off.

nodes.text: From inside the service line the open court is huge. Volley firmly into the space instead of swinging hard.
I once tried to smash a bin lid open. It is still shut, and I am still embarrassed.
Deep approach, split step, volley into the open court.
Every player needs one shot that says: not this ball, not yet. This is that shot.
They attacked and are pressing forward inside their baseline. You are scrambling wide off court, barely reaching it. What do you hit?

options.label: A flat drive down the line to pass them
options.reply: Stretched and scrambling, that is the least repeatable shot you own. Miss it and the point is simply over.

options.label: A high deep ball down the middle
options.reply: Yes. It ends their attack and buys you the time to get home.

options.label: A short angle to make them stretch
options.reply: From off court that angle lands short and central, and they are already moving forward.

nodes.text: Height is time. The higher the ball, the longer it hangs, and the further back toward home you get.
One ball doing two jobs: it takes their attack away and it walks you home.

scene.caption: One high central ball ends their attack and gives you the time to get home.

nodes.text: You reset, you recover, the next ball comes. Now what?

options.label: Go back to hitting deep cross-court with intent
options.reply: That is it. One reset, then you compete again.

options.label: Reset again and stay safe until they miss
options.reply: Two in a row and you have gone from buying time to giving it away. Safe turns passive.

nodes.text: A reset is not surrender. It is me backing away from a dog and returning later.
One high, deep, central ball. Then rejoin the rally as an equal.
Doubles now. Two of you, one line, and that line is most of the tactics.
A neutral rally ball has gone across. You are at the net, your partner is still on the baseline. Any problem?

options.label: Nothing, one up and one back covers everything
options.reply: While serving that is fine. But in a neutral rally it is a diagonal gap they can hit into all day.

options.label: You are split, so both should be up or both back
options.reply: Yes. One line, two players. Get both up when you can, or both go back.

options.label: Swap over: partner comes up, you go back
options.reply: Same shape, mirrored. The gap just moves to the other diagonal.

nodes.text: When the ball goes left, you both go left. Same distance apart, sliding together, nobody chasing alone.
Both at the net, one line, middle covered. Notice the pair moves as one shape.

scene.caption: One line, both at the net, middle covered — and the pair slides sideways together.

nodes.text: Where do most doubles points get lost?

options.label: Down the middle
options.reply: Right. Lowest net, and two players hesitating over whose ball it is.

options.label: Down the tramlines
options.reply: The tramlines look frightening, but they are a narrow, low-percentage target. Guarding them pulls you both wide.

nodes.text: The middle ball belongs to whoever can take it with a forehand at net height. Claim it — hesitation loses points nobody touched.
You're moving as a pair now. At the net while your partner serves, can you read where the return is going?
One line. Both up or both back, and the middle covered first.
You took me up on it. Good. Net play in doubles starts with an uncomfortable truth.
You're at the net. Your partner serves. You have no idea where this serve is going — and today, neither do they.
So what do you do about a serve you can't predict?

options.label: Guess a side and commit before the serve lands
options.reply: A guess moves you early and wrong half the time. The returner sees you leave and aims behind you.

options.label: Hold the middle third and read the returner instead
options.reply: Yes. The serve is a mystery; the returner isn't. Their racket tells you everything, a beat earlier.

options.label: Hug the alley so at least the line is safe
options.reply: That guards their hardest shot all day. The middle stays open, and that's where returns live.

nodes.text: Settle as the serve is struck. Split-step as the returner swings. Two beats, every point.
I can't read bin lids in flight either. So I watch the paws that open them.
Watch the returner's contact point and racket face. The ball goes where the face points — you'll know before it leaves.
The serve could land anywhere in the box. Your station doesn't care — it covers the likely reply.

scene.caption: The serve could land anywhere in this box. Your station does not care — it covers the likely reply.

nodes.text: Your partner's serves are landing short and soft today. What changes?

options.label: Start a step deeper and shelve the poach
options.reply: Right. A weak serve means a stronger return. Position for the ball you're about to get.

options.label: Poach more — someone has to save these points
options.reply: A gamble on a bad serve is two mistakes in one point. Hold, and take what you can reach.

nodes.text: Position for the return, not for the serve. Read rackets, not hopes.
The serve leaves your partner's racket and swings wide. The returner is dragged off court. Most net players slide out with them.
The wide serve is struck. Which way do you move?

options.label: Out toward your tramline
options.reply: You just covered their hardest shot: tightest strip, highest net, hit while running the other way.

options.label: Step in toward the middle
options.reply: Yes. You are standing where their best ball has to travel.

options.label: Back toward the service line
options.reply: Now you are digging half-volleys off your shoelaces. You came forward for a reason.

nodes.text: Wide drags them off the court. From out there they need the target with the most margin.
Same geometry as a baseline rally. The diagonal is longer court and lower net, straight through the middle.
The serve goes wide. Their safest reply cuts back through the middle, where you're already leaning.

scene.caption: The wide serve pulls the returner into the alley, and their safest ball is the diagonal through the middle — so you step in, not out.

nodes.text: And the return down your alley?

options.label: It beats you sometimes, and that's fine
options.reply: Right. You lose the odd point to their best shot and take their easy one all afternoon.

options.label: Split the difference, cover a bit of both
options.reply: Halfway between two jobs does neither. You arrive late in the middle and still get passed.

nodes.text: Wide serve, lean in. The middle is where their safe ball has to go.
You watch the serve go up the T. It pulls the returner toward the middle, onto the backhand, crowded for room.
No room to swing, no angle to open. What comes back?

options.label: A slow, high ball down the middle
options.reply: Usually, yes. A shortened swing sends the ball back roughly where it came from.

options.label: A sharp angle into the open court
options.reply: From the middle of the court there is no angle to find. They'd have to invent one.

options.label: A drive at your partner's feet
options.reply: That needs a full swing, and the serve just took their swing away. Waiting for it costs you the volley.

nodes.text: With less time they steer the ball instead of hitting it. Blocked returns float, over the lowest part of the net.
No swing means no angle. The reply comes back over the middle, and that one is yours.

scene.caption: No room to swing means no angle to create: the reply usually comes straight back over the lowest part of the net. That is your volley.

nodes.text: Start moving as their swing starts. Meet the ball above net height, in front of the center.
Take it late and that gift is at your ankles. I'm knee-high, so I take everything early.
You've got the volley. Where do you put it?

options.label: Down the middle, between the two of them
options.reply: Yes. Or at the feet of whichever one is closer. Simple beats clever here.

options.label: Angled into the open alley
options.reply: Smallest target, hit on the move. That's how a free point becomes your error.

nodes.text: T serve, expect the block. Move early and volley it back through the middle.
A whole service game. Three returns went past your hip through the middle. Nobody touched your alley once.
You are hugging your tramline, guarding the alley. What is wrong with that?

options.label: Nothing, the alley has to be covered
options.reply: Covered against what? The narrowest strip on court, over the highest net, hit on the run.

options.label: You defend their worst ball, leave their best one open
options.reply: That's it. The alley is their hardest shot. The middle is their easiest.

options.label: You should stand even wider
options.reply: Wider defends the shot that isn't coming, and the middle gets cheaper for them every point.

nodes.text: The middle is the lowest net, the longest space, and the seam where two players hesitate over whose ball it is.
The strip you're guarding is their tightest target. The lane you're leaving open is their easiest.

scene.caption: The strip you are guarding is the returner's tightest, highest-net target. The lane you are leaving open is their easiest one.

nodes.text: Position is only half the job. Split-step as the returner strikes and you can push off either way.
Perfect position, still feet. How much does that cover?

options.label: Only whatever happens to fly at you
options.reply: Right. Still feet are late feet, wherever they happen to be standing.

options.label: Most of it, if the position is right
options.reply: That's a statue with a good address. The ball goes past it anyway.

nodes.text: Give the alley up on purpose. Live in the middle third and split-step.
First serve missed. You poached twice this game and won both points. Tempting.
But the returner has stepped inside their baseline. Slower ball, and more time for them.
Do you go again?

options.label: Poach again, it's been working
options.reply: From in there they watch you leave and hit where you were. The slow ball gives them that time.

options.label: Hold your half, split-step, volley what comes
options.reply: Yes. Hold, and their firmer return still has to get past you.

options.label: Move right up on the net
options.reply: The extra pace arrives before you can react, and the lob over your head gets easier.

nodes.text: On a fast first serve a poach forces a decision they can't make in time. On a second serve, they can.
They've stepped in. The reply comes back firmer and lower, often at your partner's feet.

scene.caption: They have stepped in and the reply comes back firmer and lower. Stay in your half, split-step, and volley anything you can reach.

nodes.text: A second serve is slow enough to read in flight. Lean off what you see — half a step, not a lunge.
And look up. Anyone my height gets lobbed constantly. It's the one shot I see coming.
The return goes up over your head. What now?

options.label: Cross to the other half — that lob is your partner's ball
options.reply: Yes. Switch immediately and cover their side. A shout helps your partner launch, but your feet go first.

options.label: Back-pedal and swing at it over your shoulder
options.reply: That ball rarely lands, and you finish it off balance facing the wrong way.

nodes.text: Second serve: hold your half, read it in flight, and when the lob goes up — switch.
